entries.interest: The premise set has **no** satisfying row, so the argument is valid vacuously: every branch of the tree closes before the conclusion is ever consulted. This is the form on which the whole relevance-logic dispute turns, and the informational reading disagrees with the truth table here for a stateable reason -- rejecting Weakening lets a state carry inconsistent information without carrying all information. Note that in this course explosion is *not* a citable rule: the proof must spell out the reductio.

english.gloss: The barber shaves himself and does not shave himself; therefore the moon is made of cheese.

appearances.quote: Mares 2004 reads x ⊩ A & ∼A as 'x carries the information that A and not A' -- a state can carry inconsistent information without carrying all information.
Contradictions have truth-likelihood 0, hence a maximal information measure of 1. Floridi's contingency requirement gives the opposite verdict: both logical truths and contradictions measure 0.

entries.interest: A classical tautology stated purely with the conditional, and the sharpest single marker of the classical/intuitionistic boundary: it fails in every Heyting algebra with more than two elements. It is also where the Curry–Howard correspondence stops -- per SEP it 'is not the type of any combinator in the type assignment system TA_CL', so the combinators name every substructural fork *below* intuitionistic logic and nothing names the classical step above it. The proof needs a nested reductio and no shorter route is available.

english.gloss: If it is true that 'if my winning entails my losing then I win', then I win.

appearances.quote: is not the type of any combinator in the type assignment system TA_CL

course.note: ⚠ Its intuitionistic status is NOT in the SEP intuitionistic-logic entry; cite it as a textbook result.

entries.interest: The combinator **W**, and the theorem Curry's paradox uses without anyone noticing. Its ND proof is where structural contraction hides: the assumption is cited **twice** inside the subproof and discharged once, silently converting `p, p ⊢ q` into `⊢ p ⊃ q`. The classroom exercise is to ask students to count how many times the assumption is cited, then impose the affine restriction -- every assumption may be cited at most once -- and ask them to redo it. They cannot.

appearances.quote: the contraction rule A→(A→B)⇒(A→B). The role of contraction was noticed by Fitch 1936.
Fitch's basic logic K contains exactly the combinators T, B and W -- so Fitch's own system builds contraction in as a primitive constant.

course.note: Pairs with curry-contraction-only and curry-complete as a three-form set.

entries.interest: A genuine tautology in eight rows -- and, on Fitelson's diagnosis, **the accomplice in Simpson's paradox**. It licenses sliding between the *suppositional* reading ('if one is female, then treatment raises recovery') and the *conjunctive* reading ('being a female treatment-receiver raises recovery'). On Simpson's own numbers the first is true and the second is false. The classical equivalence is what makes the fallacy feel obligatory: students carry a real theorem of their home logic into a setting where the corresponding equivalence fails.

english.gloss: 'If it rains, then if the drain is blocked the cellar floods' says the same as 'if it rains and the drain is blocked, the cellar floods'.

appearances.quote: while the suppositional reading allows for association reversals, on the conjunctive reading it cannot be the case both that being a female treatment-receiver and being a male treatment-receiver raises the probability of recovery, but being a treatment receiver simpliciter does not.

course.note: Good Lecture 1 provocation; pairs with simpson-amalgamation.

entries.interest: **The Lecture 1 provocation.** `c` = the conclusion's information is contained in the premises; `n` = information-gain requires ruling out possibilities not already ruled out; `s` = the conclusion rules out something new; `i` = the deduction is informative. Exactly one of sixteen rows satisfies all four premises, and in it `i` is false. The scandal is not a paradox or a confusion -- it is a **valid argument from plausible premises to a conclusion that is obviously false**. So a premise must go, and the whole literature is the fight over which one. Run the table on the board in three minutes, then ask the class which premise they want to keep.

english.gloss: Deduction only makes explicit what the premises already contain; and you learn something only by ruling out a possibility you had not already ruled out; so deduction never teaches you anything.

appearances.quote: logical truths have a truth-likelihood of 1, and therefore an information measure of 0.
Deductions are informative for us precisely because we are not logically omniscient.

course.note: ⚠ Hintikka's standard reply does NOT cover this course: on his measure every propositional and monadic deduction measures 0. The response that does is D'Agostino & Floridi 2009.

entries.interest: Curry's paradox needs **two** things and each alone is harmless. This is the version with both: the contraction half `c ⊃ (c ⊃ p)` gives you the *conditional*, the fixed-point half `(c ⊃ p) ⊃ c` gives you the *sentence* (by Peirce's Law it already yields `c`), and only together do they deliver `p` -- and then anything downstream of `p`. Compare **curry-contraction-only**, which is the same argument with the second half replaced by the W axiom: it is invalid, and the tree stays open at `c = F`.

english.gloss: Let C be the sentence 'if this very sentence is true, then Yale is in Ohio.'

appearances.quote: Either variant of Curry's paradox is positive, in the sense that it relies on one or two theorems of the positive implicational logic of David Hilbert.

course.note: Teach as a pair with curry-contraction-only: the invalid one first.

entries.interest: Two rows, and it is the whole of Russell's paradox once the set theory is stripped away. Tennant's derivation of naive comprehension from Basic Law V ends exactly here: instantiate at `y ∉ y`, get `r ∈ r ≡ r ∉ r`, and this refutes it 'within a very weak propositional logic'. It is also the first row of the fixed-point table -- the Liar's premise is **unsatisfiable**, which is precisely what makes Curry (whose premise is satisfiable) the worse paradox.

entries.interest: A finding, not just an exercise. Pollock distinguishes **rebutting** defeaters (which give you reason for the denial) from **undercutting** ones (which give you reason to doubt that the premises support the conclusion *here*). Reify the support relation as `s` and materialise the prima facie link, and rebutting turns out to **entail** undercutting -- run modus tollens back through the link. The converse fails (see **undercut-not-denial**). So `⊃` does not merely blur Pollock's distinction; it collapses it in **one direction only**. That is a sharper criticism of the material conditional than the usual one.

english.gloss: The object is illuminated by red light, so it isn't really red; it looks red and looking red normally supports being red; so looking red does not support being red here.

appearances.quote: undercutting defeaters give one a reason for doubting that the usual relationship between the premises and the conclusion hold in the given case.

course.note: Teach with undercut-not-denial as a valid/invalid pair.

earliest_lecture.note: falsum appears, so no earlier than Lecture 10

names: The paradox of backward induction, epistemic core
entries.interest: Eight rows, none of them satisfying, and **every one of the four premises is needed** -- deleting any single one restores satisfiability (3, 1, 1, 1 rows respectively). `d` = the player deviated from the backward-induction move; `k` = she is still taken to be rational at the off-path node; `p` = she is rational. The deviation both licenses the rationality assumption (Aumann) and refutes it. The payoff is that **each named resolution in the literature drops exactly one member of this set, one each, with no overlap**: Aumann drops `d`, Bicchieri drops `d ⊃ k`, Stalnaker drops `k ⊃ p`, Selten drops `d ⊃ ∼p`. Four premises, four positions, one truth table.

english.gloss: She played the irrational move; we still credit her with rationality; credited rationality is rationality; but playing that move is irrational.

appearances.quote: Suppose some player has deviated from her Backward Induction strategy as computed in pre-game deliberation. What are others to make of this? Answers offered in the literature range from interpreting the deviation as an error without any future implications (Aumann 1995) to treating it as significant in various ways (Bicchieri 1993).

course.note: The best minimal-inconsistent-set exercise in the catalogue. Set the four deletions as sub-questions.

entries.interest: Hájek's point made literal: the Dutch book argument's potential sure *loss* is symmetric with a possible sure *gain*, so there is a parallel 'Czech Book Argument' concluding that one ought to **violate** the probability calculus. Run the normative bridge in both directions and the position is inconsistent -- every branch closes in 32 rows. Delete `g_s ⊃ o_n` and it reopens, which is exactly Hájek's own recorded repair (reformulate so the agent should accept bets that are 'either fair or favorable'). A good 'find the premise whose removal reopens the tree' exercise, and it teaches that a valid argument to ⊥ **refutes its premise set** rather than proving anything.

appearances.quote: the potential sure loss is symmetric with a possible sure gain. As Hájek emphasizes, there is a corresponding 'Czech Book Argument', which parallels the DBA, with the conclusion that one ought to violate the probability calculus.

names: The set-theoretic distributive law, finite case
entries.interest: **The best way to introduce the Axiom of Choice to a first-year.** This is the finite case of the set-theoretic distributive law that is *equivalent* to AC: pick one member from each of two non-empty sets. It is a plain tautology in sixteen rows, and the three-sets version is a tautology in sixty-four. The right-hand disjunction has |J|^|I| disjuncts, so for finite I your students can check it on a table. **AC is precisely the claim that this stays true when the disjunction becomes infinitely long** -- at which point it is no longer a tautology and no longer even expressible. AC is a tautology that ran out of room. Contrast the tempting mis-statement `((p∨q) & (r∨s)) ⊃ ((p&r) ∨ (q&s))`, which is invalid in two rows: the choice function must be allowed to choose *independently* in each set.

english.gloss: There is an apple or a pear in the first bowl, and an apple or a pear in the second; so there is some pair, one from each bowl.

appearances.quote: The set-theoretic distributive law is listed among the equivalents of AC over ZF.
For every set A of pairwise-disjoint non-empty sets, there exists a set that contains exactly one element from each set in A.

course.note: Long ∨E-heavy proof -- a good end-of-unit Fitch exercise. AC is NOT the quantifier shift; that confusion is its own predicate-logic entry.

entries.interest: Classically valid with **no countermodel** in either direction. That matters, because the widespread remark that distribution 'fails in quantum logic' is not a claim about any row of this table: it is a claim about the **lattice** identity `a ∧ (b∨c) ≤ (a∧b) ∨ (a∧c)` in the orthomodular lattice `L(H)` of closed subspaces of a Hilbert space, where join is **span**, not union. Only that direction fails; the converse is free in any lattice. In `L(H)`, a disjunction can be certain while neither disjunct is even possible -- the span of two lines contains every superposition of them.

english.gloss: Spin-x is up, and spin-z is either up or down; so either (spin-x up and spin-z up) or (spin-x up and spin-z down).

appearances.quote: Since a typical closed subspace has infinitely many complementary closed subspaces, this lattice is not distributive.

appearances.who: Birkhoff & von Neumann, reported by Wilce
appearances.quote: Immediately this proposal faces the problem that the lattice L(H) is not distributive, making it impossible to give these 'quantum' connectives a truth-functional interpretation.
Dummett 1978 -- who was not a proponent -- considered restricting ∨-elimination so that distribution is no longer derivable.

entries.interest: AGM's most debated postulate, as a formal object. Hansson: having contracted 'Cleopatra had a son or a daughter' on learning the book was a novel, 'I learn from a reliable source that Cleopatra had a child. It seems perfectly reasonable for me to then add `p ∨ q` to my set of beliefs **without also reintroducing either `p` or `q`**. This contradicts Recovery.' Zero of thirty-two rows survive: **the classical diagnosis of a Recovery-respecting reasoner on this case is 'your beliefs are inconsistent.'** Its converse, with Recovery removed, is **cleopatra-without-recovery** -- invalid, and its unique open branch is exactly the epistemic state Hansson describes.

appearances.quote: It seems perfectly reasonable for me to then add p ∨ q to my set of beliefs without also reintroducing either p or q. This contradicts Recovery.

course.note: Teach as a pair with cleopatra-without-recovery: same apparatus, opposite verdicts, and the difference is logical closure.

names: Kant's argument against empirical moral theory
entries.interest: **Kant's argument, and the course's spine.** It is the one form worked by all three methods in the handouts themselves: the truth table in Lecture 4, the tree in Lecture 8, the natural deduction in Lecture 10. A three-link chain whose end negates its own start, so the tree closes on all four branches and the proof is a clean reductio with no nesting beyond depth one. Structurally this is *consequentia mirabilis* wearing a chain: anything that implies its own negation is false.

english.gloss: If I trust the memo I act on it; if I act on it I go public; if I go public I should not have trusted the memo. So I should not trust the memo.

appearances.quote: If a moral theory is studied empirically then examples of conduct will be considered. And if examples of conduct are considered, principles for selecting examples will be used. But if principles for selecting examples are used, then moral theory is not being studied empirically. Therefore, moral theory is not studied empirically.
Exercise: Confirm the validity of this argument using the tree method.

canonical.distinguishes: premise order and multiplicity, renaming of atoms, and classical equivalence of each sentence (so double-negation variants share an ID)

names: The Dutch book argument, as SEP states it
entries.interest: SEP numbers the argument explicitly: premises (1)–(3) are **descriptive** and conclusion (4) is **normative**, and the truth table locates the gap to a single row of thirty-two. `b_l` = credences are linked to betting quotients; `v` = the credences violate the probability axioms; `k` = a cunning bettor can make book; `l_s` = she is open to a sure loss; `o` = she ought to be coherent. Adding one premise, `l_s ⊃ o`, makes it valid -- and that premise is normative, is nowhere in (1)–(3), and **is the whole is/ought gap in a single conditional.**
entries.countermodel_gloss: The unique open branch is a world where she violates the axioms, her credences *are* linked to her betting quotients, a bookie *can* make book, she *is* open to a sure loss -- **and she is still under no obligation to be coherent.** That branch is not our invention; it is the entry's own objection.

english.gloss: Your credences fix your betting odds; incoherent credences let a bookie guarantee himself a profit; being exploitable that way is a sure loss. So you ought to be coherent.

appearances.quote: (1) for an agent with degree of belief q in M a bet on or against M at corresponding odds will be acceptable... But then (2) by the Dutch Book theorem a cunning bettor could assure himself a profit from someone who violates the probability axioms. Since (3) violating the axioms leaves the bettor open to being Dutch Booked… it is concluded that (4) one ought to satisfy the probability axioms.
If the threat of such a loss is seen as unlikely... then it is hard to see why the mere potential of a sure loss should demand coherence.

course.note: The form exactly as SEP states it. **The classroom version is `dutch-book-lecture-form`**, which strengthens the third premise to `(b_l&k) > (l_s&d)` -- see that entry for why.

nd.note: No derivation exists. Every attempt stalls at the same place: `o` occurs in no premise, so no rule can ever introduce it. That syntactic observation is arguably the cleanest formal statement of Hume's gap this course can offer.

display.sequent: b_l, v ⊃ k, (b_l & k) ⊃ l_s  ⊭ v ⊃ o

canonical.distinguishes: premise order and multiplicity, renaming of atoms, and classical equivalence of each sentence (so double-negation variants share an ID)

names: The Dutch book argument, Lecture 7/8 form
entries.interest: **The shared Lecture 7/8 worked example**, and a good illustration of tuning a form to a teaching job without damaging it. It strengthens `dutch-book-is-ought`'s third premise from `(b&k) ⊃ l` to `(b&k) ⊃ (l & d)`, where `d` = you are also in for a difficult conversation. Three things follow. The premise is now strictly **stronger** (verified: it entails the original), so the argument failing is more striking, not less. The countermodel is still **unique**, now one row in sixty-four rather than one in thirty-two. And the open branch now carries a **conjunction** to resolve, so the walk up that branch in Lecture 7 illustrates four tree rules rather than three, and its lowest complex formula is a *descendant* rather than a root -- which is the shape the handout's induction wants.
entries.countermodel_gloss: The single open branch is an agent who violates the probability axioms, whose odds really are fixed by her degrees of belief, against whom a bookie really can make book, who really is open to a sure loss **and** a difficult conversation --- and who is nonetheless under no obligation to change her mind. Every descriptive premise holds; the normative conclusion fails. Adding `l ⊃ o` closes the tree (verified).

english.gloss: Your degrees of belief fix which betting odds you find acceptable. If your betting odds violate the probability axioms, a cunning bettor can make a Dutch book against those odds. If your degrees of belief fix your odds and a bettor can make book against them, then you are open to a sure loss and a difficult conversation. Therefore, if your degrees of belief violate the probability axioms, you ought to change them.

appearances.who: Ramsey and de Finetti, after SEP's numbering
appearances.quote: (1) for an agent with degree of belief q in M a bet on or against M at corresponding odds will be acceptable... (2) by the Dutch Book theorem a cunning bettor could assure himself a profit from someone who violates the probability axioms... it is concluded that (4) one ought to satisfy the probability axioms.
Exercise: Consider the argument with premises X: b and v ⊃ k and (b & k) ⊃ (l & d), and with conclusion A: v ⊃ o. Use a tree to show that this argument is tree-invalid.

course.note: **The shared invalid argument for Lectures 7 and 8, and it must stay shared**: L7 runs it forward (open branch to countermodel) for completeness, L8 runs the *same* argument backward (countermodel to open branch) for soundness. Two different arguments would break the point that these are two directions of one fact. Tree: 1 open, 3 closed, depth 3; opens with a non-branching negated-conditional step seeding two literals; the open branch resolves a conjunction and determines all six atoms, so no atom is left unconstrained. Rules exercised on the tracked branch: negated conditional, conditional (twice), conjunction --- plus negated conjunction off it, which illustrates the easy clause in the Lemma 3 proof. The syntactic hint to give after they finish: `o` occurs in no premise.

nd.note: No derivation exists, and the reason is worth teaching: `o` occurs in no premise, so no rule can ever introduce it. That is arguably the cleanest formal statement of Hume's gap this course can offer.

display.sequent: b, v ⊃ k, (b & k) ⊃ (l & d)  ⊭ v ⊃ o

canonical.distinguishes: premise order and multiplicity, renaming of atoms, and classical equivalence of each sentence (so double-negation variants share an ID)

entries.interest: The same argument with the **normative bridge already granted** (`l_s ⊃ o` is a premise here) and it is *still* invalid, because the sure loss requires that the agent actually accept the bets. A student who finds the open branch has independently rediscovered the standard objection in the literature; adding `a` -- Jackson and Pargetter's 'forced betting situations', in which the agent is required to post betting quotients and then to place bets with them -- makes it valid.
entries.countermodel_gloss: The unique open branch sets `a = F`: **she simply refuses to bet.** SEP §1.4 puts it in exactly those words -- 'the agent can always prevent a sure loss by simply refusing to bet.' The open branch *is* the refusal.

appearances.quote: the agent can always prevent a sure loss by simply refusing to bet.
forced betting situations, in which the agent is required to post betting quotients, and then to place bets with those quotients.

nd.note: No derivation. The failed attempt is instructive: you can get `k` by CondE, but `(k & a) ⊃ l_s` needs `a`, and nothing yields it.

display.sequent: v ⊃ k, (k & a) ⊃ l_s, l_s ⊃ o, v  ⊭ o

canonical.distinguishes: premise order and multiplicity, renaming of atoms, and classical equivalence of each sentence (so double-negation variants share an ID)

entries.interest: Robert says the elephant beside him looks pink; but Robert's colour vision becomes unreliable in the presence of pink elephants. Ordinarily 'looks pink' would support 'is pink' -- and that very conclusion undercuts the support. **The classical verdict exactly reproduces the philosophical verdict: the argument warrants nothing.** `p` does not follow, `∼p` does not follow (see **pink-elephant-not-p**), and all three surviving rows share `s = F`. Self-defeat here is not a stipulation but a **theorem**: the premises entail `p ⊃ ∼s`, and adding `s` makes the set unsatisfiable.
entries.countermodel_gloss: Both open branches set `s = F` -- the support relation has been destroyed by the argument's own conclusion. That is what self-defeat *is*, drawn rather than asserted.

english.gloss: It looks pink to Robert. If looking pink supports being pink and it looks pink, then it is pink. If it is pink, Robert's colour vision is unreliable here. If his vision is unreliable, looking pink does not support being pink.

appearances.quote: An argument is self-defeating if it supports a defeater for one of its own defeasible steps. Here is an interesting example: (1) Robert says that the elephant beside him looks pink. (2) Robert's color vision becomes unreliable in the presence of pink elephants.

course.note: Strong candidate for the shared Lecture 7/8 argument: 4 atoms, 16 rows, and the companion form makes 'refute both, then find what does follow' available.

nd.note: No derivation. Note what *is* derivable: `p ⊃ ∼s` (valid), and `⊥` once `s` is added as a premise.

display.sequent: l, (s & l) ⊃ p, p ⊃ u, u ⊃ ∼s  ⊭ p

canonical.distinguishes: premise order and multiplicity, renaming of atoms, and classical equivalence of each sentence (so double-negation variants share an ID)

entries.interest: Six premises, five atoms, and **four genuinely different connectives including a biconditional**. `s_d` = the court stated it; `c_d` = the court expressly formulated it as its ratio; `n_d` = it belongs to the ratio; `o_d` = it is obiter; `b_d` = it binds later courts. The twist SEP records is that 'even if a court chooses to explicitly formulate the *ratio* of its decision, this precise formulation is not itself regarded as binding on later courts.' Adding `n_d` makes it valid.
entries.countermodel_gloss: The single open branch has a name in the law: **the court said it, the court called it its holding, and it was still obiter, because it was not necessary to the result.** The countermodel is not an artefact of the encoding; it is the doctrine.

english.gloss: A ruling binds exactly when it is part of the ratio. The court stated this, and expressly called it its ratio. Anything stated is either ratio or obiter, and obiter does not bind. So it binds.

appearances.work: Precedent and Analogy in Legal Reasoning
appearances.quote: even if a court chooses to explicitly formulate the ratio of its decision, this precise formulation is not itself regarded as binding on later courts.

appearances.work: Precedent and Analogy in Legal Reasoning
appearances.quote: The ratio of a case represents the 'holding' or 'ruling'… Obiter dicta, by contrast, represent other statements and views expressed in the judgment which are not binding.

course.note: Candidate for the shared Lecture 7/8 argument if connective variety is the deciding criterion: it is the only entry using ≡, ∨, ⊃ and ∼ together.

nd.note: No derivation. BicondE on premise 1 needs `n_d`, and the ∨E on `n_d | o_d` fails on the obiter side.

display.sequent: b_d ≡ n_d, s_d, c_d, c_d ⊃ s_d, n_d ∨ o_d, o_d ⊃ ∼b_d  ⊭ b_d

canonical.distinguishes: premise order and multiplicity, renaming of atoms, and classical equivalence of each sentence (so double-negation variants share an ID)

entries.interest: The rhetorical form of Simpson's paradox: treatment beats control among men (`a_m`), and among women (`a_w`), and the patient is certainly one or the other -- so surely treatment is better overall (`a_p`)? It is not. **The open branches name the confounder**: both set `h = F`, where `h` is the row-homogeneity of the subgroup weights that SEP §2.2 shows is necessary for reversal. Note that the premise `m ∨ ∼m` is completely **idle** -- and, read as a claim about people rather than about sentence letters, it is also **contestable**, which is a second and independent reason not to lean on it -- worth setting as a sub-question, since noticing that excluded middle contributes nothing is the moment the 'but she's either male or female!' rhetoric loses its grip.
entries.countermodel_gloss: Two open branches, differing only in `m`, both with `h = F`: the subgroups are weighted differently in the treatment and control arms. The branch *is* the confounding variable.

english.gloss: The treatment beat the placebo among men, and among women; the patient is either a man or a woman; so the treatment beat the placebo.

appearances.quote: Should we use the treatment or not?... it does not look like the right thing to do when we don't know the patient's gender — although we know that the patient is either male or female!
Simpson's Paradox is not a paradox in the sense of presenting an inconsistent set of plausible propositions of which at least one must be rejected.

course.note: ⚠ Simpson does NOT refute proof by cases; the sure-thing schema is a tautology. The logic is the accomplice, not the victim -- see `exportation`. ⚠ Second caution, and it should be said aloud when this is set: the premise `m ∨ ∼m` is not merely idle, it is **contestable**. Read as a claim about people rather than about sentence letters, 'the patient is either male or female' is an exhaustive-and-exclusive binary that many students will reject, and they are entitled to. Nothing in the argument needs it -- the deletion test shows it does no work at all -- so the right response is to strike it rather than defend it. The source's rhetorical flourish ('although we know that the patient is either male or female!') is best quoted as the entry's wording, not adopted as the course's.

nd.note: No derivation. The fourth premise needs `h`, and nothing supplies it; `m ∨ ∼m` cannot be used for anything at all.

entries.interest: When the undercutter fires, **neither `q` nor `∼q` follows** -- two open branches differing only in `q`. That pair of branches *is* Pollock's distinction: undercutting returns you to agnosticism, rebutting pushes you to the denial. Set both directions and let students read the difference off the trees. Compare **rebut-entails-undercut**, which is valid: the material conditional collapses Pollock's distinction in one direction only.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `s = F, u = T, q = T`: the support relation is undercut and the conclusion happens to be true anyway. Losing your reason for believing something is not acquiring a reason against it.

english.gloss: It looks red; looking red normally supports being red; but the lighting is red, and red lighting undercuts that support. So it isn't red.

appearances.quote: undercutting defeaters give one a reason for doubting that the usual relationship between the premises and the conclusion hold in the given case. (Pollock 1987, 484)

nd.note: No derivation of `∼q`, and none of `q` either — that is the whole point.

entries.interest: **The cleanest 'invisible premise made visible' pair in the whole catalogue**, and it is SEP's own worked example, asserted there as a case of joint knowledge. One friend knows she is at home or at work; another knows she is at work or at the cafe; together, surely, they know she is at work. Propositionally it is invalid in one row of eight. The missing premise is 'a person is in one place at a time'; add `∼(h & c)` and it is valid. Three atoms, one open branch, nothing epistemic lost -- and the branch **names the premise the reader supplied without noticing**.

english.gloss: Ann knows Bea is at home or at work. Cal knows Bea is at work or at the cafe. So between them they know Bea is at work.

entries.interest: Harman's complaint in one table -- and note *what* it shows: `b_q = F` survives even in the rows where `p` and `q` are both true and the material conditional holds. **The belief atoms are truth-functionally sealed off from their contents.** Logic gives you `p, p ⊃ q ⊨ q`; it gives you nothing at all about `Bp, B(p ⊃ q) ⊨ Bq`. AGM's Closure postulate does not *derive* the missing link, it **stipulates** it, which is why AGM presupposes Harman's gap rather than closing it.
entries.countermodel_gloss: Three open branches, one of them with `p` and `q` both true: she believes the premise, believes the conditional, the conditional is true, and she has simply not put them together. No rule of logic obliges her to.

english.gloss: She believes the axioms and believes that they imply Fermat's theorem, and they do. So she believes Fermat's theorem.

appearances.quote: which is clearly an unrealistic idealization, since it means that the agent is taken to be 'logically omniscient'.
AGM is not really logic; it is a theory about theories.

entries.interest: The characteristic axiom of **Abelian logic** -- the converse of assertion (`A ⊃ ((A ⊃ B) ⊃ B)`, which is the combinator **T** and is classically valid). Adopting it as a schema is what makes a logic Abelian, and it is classically refuted by a single row. A clean two-atom demonstration that a plausible-looking converse can fail while its original is a theorem.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `p = F, q = T`. With `q` true the inner conditional `(p ⊃ q) ⊃ q` is true regardless of `p`, so the whole thing collapses to 'therefore `p`' with nothing supporting it.

appearances.quote: Abelian logic takes ((A→B)→B)→A as an axiom; its algebraic models are lattice-ordered abelian groups.

course.note: ⚠ Premise-free and single-connective, which is why it is a poor fit for Lectures 7/8 as it stands. To use it, make it one premise inside a chain, the way `curry-contraction-only` embeds the W axiom.

nd.note: No derivation; the tree closes on the `q`-true branch only.

names: Every function has a fixed point
entries.interest: The propositional shadow of the **combinatory fixed point theorem**. `Y x ▷ x(Y x)` means `Y` maps an `A ⊃ A` to an `A`, so its type schema would have to be `(A ⊃ A) ⊃ A`. It is a non-theorem, refuted by one row -- **but since `A ⊃ A` *is* a theorem, adopting it as a schema yields every `A` whatever** (verified: `p ⊃ p, (p ⊃ p) ⊃ p ⊨ p` is valid). So 'every function has a fixed point' has an exact propositional shadow, and the shadow is **triviality**. This is the propositional face of the fact that first-order logic expanded with combinators is inconsistent.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `p = F`. The antecedent `p ⊃ p` is a tautology, so the conditional just asserts `p` outright — and the open branch is any world where `p` is false.

appearances.quote: if we consider the language of FOL expanded with combinators, then the resulting system is inconsistent, because CL is powerful enough to define the fixed point of any function.

course.note: One-branch tree; excellent as the smallest entry that carries a real result.

nd.note: No derivation. Note the contrast: with `p ⊃ p` *and* `(p ⊃ p) ⊃ p` as premises, `p` follows in two lines.

entries.interest: **Contraction alone does not produce Curry's paradox**, and this is the proof. The W axiom is supplied here as an explicit premise, and the tree still stays open. Replace it with the *other* half of the biconditional, `(c ⊃ p) ⊃ c`, and the argument becomes valid (**curry-complete**). So the paradox needs **both** the contraction step and the fixed-point step, and each alone is refutable by tree: the second half gives you the *sentence* (by Peirce's Law it already yields `c`), the first gives you the *conditional*, and only together do they give you `p`.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `c = F, p = F, q = F`. The Curry sentence is simply false, the contraction axiom is satisfied vacuously, and nothing follows. No paradox.

appearances.quote: The role of contraction was noticed by Fitch 1936.

course.note: Teach before curry-complete. The invalid one first is the whole pedagogy.

nd.note: No derivation. You can reach `c ⊃ p` from the first two premises by CondE, and then stop: nothing yields `c`.

entries.interest: Two atoms, four rows, one countermodel -- and it is the propositional core of a real result in game semantics. Knowing that two options are not *both* the case does not tell you that exactly one is: they may both fail. In IF logic this is the failure of determinacy, where a sentence is true iff player 2 has a winning strategy and false iff player 1 does, and **neither may have one**. The entry is emphatic that this failure involves no third truth-value and no postulated gap: 'non-determinacy corresponds to a structural property: the fact that certain kinds of functions do not exist on the model considered.'
entries.countermodel_gloss: `a = F, b = F`: neither player has a winning strategy. The analogy for students is that '√2 ∈ ℚ' is not made third-truth-valued by the non-existence of a rational square root of 2 — bivalence fails here in the same style that a *solution* fails to exist.

english.gloss: It is not the case that both players have a winning strategy. So one has one exactly if the other does not.

appearances.quote: it does not fail due to the postulation of a third truth-value or a truth-value gap… Rather, the failure is a consequence of the basic assumptions of the entire semantic theory. Non-determinacy corresponds to a structural property: the fact that certain kinds of functions do not exist on the model considered.

course.note: The converse `a ≡ ∼b ⊨ ∼(a & b)` is valid — set both.

nd.note: No derivation. BicondI requires both directions and the ∼b-to-a direction has no support.

entries.interest: The textbook fallacy with a real dress. SEP: 'the more accurate statements of the doctrine of precedent are to the effect that a later court must either **follow** or **distinguish** a binding precedent -- a **disjunctive obligation**.' It does not follow from a court's distinguishing a precedent that it has not followed it, until you add that the two are exclusive -- and that exclusivity comes straight from the entry's own definition of distinguishing as 'a precedent **not being followed**'.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `f = T, d = T`: it did both. Whether that is possible is a substantive question about the doctrine, and the open branch is where you have to answer it.

english.gloss: The court must either follow the precedent or distinguish it. It distinguished it. So it did not follow it.

appearances.work: Precedent and Analogy in Legal Reasoning
appearances.quote: a later court must either follow or distinguish a binding precedent — a disjunctive obligation.

course.note: ⚠ The course has no deontic operator, so `Ob(F ∨ D)` versus `Ob(F) ∨ Ob(D)` — the whole content of the doctrine — is invisible here.

entries.interest: **The best form in the catalogue for showing that LEM is not a fact about the connectives.** The two biconditional premises *are* the team-semantics satisfaction rule for literals, applied to a two-assignment team: `X ⊨ x=y` iff *every* assignment in `X` agrees, and `X ⊨ x≠y` iff every assignment disagrees. Four of sixteen rows are coherent, and in two of them **both** disjuncts fail. The moral: LEM is a fact about **evaluating at a single point**. Move the evaluation point to a *set* and it goes, with no change to any connective and no non-classical machinery smuggled in -- the whole thing is a classical truth table.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `p_1 = T, p_2 = F` (and the mirror). A team containing one assignment on which `x=y` and one on which it fails satisfies neither `x=y` nor `x≠y`. SEP states it exactly so.

english.gloss: In every world I hold open, x is y — or in every world I hold open, x is not y.

appearances.quote: if a team X contains both assignments s with s(x)=s(y) and assignments s′ with s′(x)≠s′(y) then X ⊭ x=y and X ⊭ x≠y.

nd.note: No derivation. Neither BicondE gives you a disjunct without a premise about `p_1`, `p_2`.

entries.interest: **The course's current shared Lecture 7/8 invalid argument, recorded here for comparison.** Structurally it is well built and that is exactly why it is hard to replace: 4 atoms and 16 rows (small enough to display a table row), a negated-conditional conclusion that resolves without branching and seeds two atoms immediately, one branch that **closes** and three that stay **open**, and a development that exercises the ∼⊃, ∨, ∼∨, & and ⊃ rules in that order. Lecture 7 runs it *open branch → countermodel* for completeness; Lecture 8 runs the very same argument *countermodel → open branch* for soundness. Its only defect is that it is philosophically arbitrary.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `p = T, s = F, r = T`, with `q` free. It names nothing — which is the whole complaint.

appearances.quote: Exercise: Consider the argument with premises X: ∼(p∨q)∨(r&∼s) and s⊃(r∨q) and with conclusion A: p⊃s. Use a tree to show that this argument is tree-invalid.

course.note: **Superseded by `dutch-book-is-ought` in the V2.0 handouts.** Kept as the benchmark: any candidate for this slot must match its structural profile -- 4 atoms, at least one closing branch, at least one open branch, and a non-branching first step. Its one advantage over the replacement is rule variety: its development exercises the negated-conditional, disjunction, negated-disjunction, conjunction and conditional rules, where the Dutch book exercises only three.

entries.interest: `dutch-book-is-ought` with its one missing premise supplied: **`l_s ⊃ o`, one ought not be open to a sure loss.** That premise is normative, it appears nowhere in SEP's numbered premises (1)–(3), and adding it is the whole difference between an invalid argument and a valid one. Every one of the four premises is load-bearing here (verified by deletion). **This is the is/ought gap as a single conditional**, and the pair is the exercise: run the invalid version first, find the one open branch in thirty-two rows, then ask what would have to be added.

english.gloss: …and one ought not leave oneself open to a guaranteed loss.

appearances.quote: If the threat of such a loss is seen as unlikely... then it is hard to see why the mere potential of a sure loss should demand coherence.

canonical.distinguishes: premise order and multiplicity, renaming of atoms, and classical equivalence of each sentence (so double-negation variants share an ID)

names: The Dutch book, Lecture 7/8 form, repaired
entries.interest: The classroom form with the normative bridge `l ⊃ o` supplied. **Lecture 7 sets this as the follow-up exercise** --- "Add that as a fourth premise, `l ⊃ o`, and the tree closes. (Try it.)" All four premises are load-bearing, and note that `d` is carried through the derivation without ever being used: the difficult conversation is real but idle, which is worth a remark when the tree closes.

appearances.quote: Add that as a fourth premise, l ⊃ o, and the tree closes. (Try it.)

course.note: The repair target for dutch-book-lecture-form. Setting it as homework closes the loop on the is/ought point.

names: Distributed knowledge, with the invisible premise supplied
entries.interest: The two-witness argument becomes valid the moment you add the premise every reader supplied without noticing: **a person is in one place at a time.** Three atoms, and the whole point is the contrast with the invalid original --- the open branch there set `h = T` and `c = T`, which is absurd about people and perfectly fine about sentence letters. **The cleanest "invisible premise made visible" pair in the catalogue.** The ND proof is a good `∨E` workout with a reductio nested inside it.

english.gloss: Ann knows Bea is at home or at work; Cal knows she is at work or at the cafe; and nobody is in two places at once. So she is at work.

appearances.quote: The entry gives the two-agent case as an illustration of distributed knowledge; the exclusivity premise is left tacit.

course.note: The repair target for distributed-knowledge. Teach the invalid one first; the open branch names the missing premise.

earliest_lecture.note: falsum appears, so no earlier than Lecture 10

display.sequent: h ∨ w, w ∨ c, ∼(h & c)  ⊨ w

entries.interest: The combinator **T**, `Txy ▷ yx`, and a classical tautology. It is worth having beside `abelian-axiom`, which is its **converse** `((p ⊃ q) ⊃ q) ⊃ p` and is invalid in a single row. Adopting the converse as a schema is what makes a logic Abelian; keeping only this direction is what everyone else does. A clean two-atom demonstration that a plausible-looking converse can fail while its original is a theorem.

english.gloss: If it is raining, then if it's true that rain implies wet streets, the streets are wet.

appearances.quote: Fitch's basic logic K contains exactly the combinators T, B and W.

course.note: Set with abelian-axiom as a valid/invalid converse pair.
